## Fundamental MR measurements

<!--
![Fundamental MR measurements.](images/ch05/fundamental-mr-measurements.png){#fig-ch05-fundamental-mr-measurements}
-->

In this section we review the relationship between the programming parameters and the physical measurements of magnetic resonance we measure. Finally, we describe how these parameters appear in the images we produce.

* Pulse sequence programming
* Fundamental MR parameters
* Image contrast

## Pulse sequency programming

![The main elements we control in the MR instrument (McRobbie et al., *MRI: From Picture to Proton*, 2e, Fig. 9.1).](images/ch05/pulse-sequency-programming.png){#fig-ch05-pulse-sequency-programming}
The instrument components we control are the signals on the RF coil transmission and the large imaging gradients. We control both the amplitudes and timing of those signals.  The steady state field ($B_0$) is not varied, though we might notice some of its imperfections and try to calibrate them out using a method called **shimming**.

But the programming is principally designed to control the gradients and RF signal. The orchestration of the signal amplitudes and timing is called 88pulse sequence programming**'**. The three tabs in this image show screen shots with the various parameters we set to control the actions of the pulse sequence.

## MR pulse sequences

![MR pulse sequences.](images/ch05/mr-pulse-sequences.png){#fig-ch05-mr-pulse-sequences}

This diagram shows a conventional way we represent the pulse sequence.  A classic sequence, called Spin Echo, is shown.  We will learn about this particular sequence later.  For now, just notice that the horizontal axis refers to time and each of the lines shows one of the parameters we control in the sequence. 

By choosing different parameters, we measure different MR parameters that reveal different features of the substrate (brain, in our case). The pulse sequence can be adjusted to highlight certain differences and diminish others.

The MR images that we produce are not at all what you see if you look at the brain with your eye. The MR images represent magnetic resonance quantities that **WE DO NOT SEE**.  These measurements of the magnetic field determined by properties of the tissue. The images represent the otherwise invisible physical properties.

## MR quantities (weighted)

![MR quantities (weighted).](images/ch05/mr-quantities-weighted.png){#fig-ch05-mr-quantities-weighted}

An important aspect of magnetic resonance is that the same instrument can be programmed to measure different MR signals. This slide shows three images from a similar slice of a brain, obtained using three different pulse sequences. The three sequences measure different fundamental physical properties of the tissue.

## MR pulse sequence parameter choices

![MR pulse sequence parameter choices.](images/ch05/mr-pulse-sequence-parameter-choices.png){#fig-ch05-mr-pulse-sequence-parameter-choices}

Even when using a single basic pulse sequence, altering the parameters can emphasize different physical properties of the system. In this image, the authors used a spin echo type sequence to produce the array of images at the right.  The sequence timing parameters are varied, and each set of parameters produces a different signal and thus different image. By selecting different parameters we measure different signals; these signals depend on different tissue properties.  

The main point of these images is to show you that the MR instrument is quite flexible. The same instrument can be programmed to measure different aspects of the tissue under study.

## To the future – and beyond

![To the future – and beyond.](images/ch05/to-the-future-and-beyond.png){#fig-ch05-to-the-future-and-beyond}

Much is known about the relationship between the sequence, its parameters, and the underlying tissue.  But this field is certainly not finished.  New discoveries continue to be made and people invent new ideas about pulse sequences that enable us to measure new things.  One of the main topics of this course, measuring functional signals from the brain, was only invented thirty years ago. Many new ideas continue to emerge.

## MR: Free induction decay

![MR: Free induction decay.](images/ch05/mr-free-induction-decay.png){#fig-ch05-mr-free-induction-decay}

In this section we cover the most basic of MR signals, a signal that is the foundation of all other magnetic resonance signals: **free induction decay**.  Nearly everything else we do will be based on understanding this signal.

## The free induction decay experiment

::: {.panel-tabset}

## The substrate

![The substrate, in this case a beaker of water, is placed in a uniform magnetic field.](images/ch05/the-free-induction-decay-experiment-1.png){#fig-ch05-the-free-induction-decay-experiment-1 fig-cap-location="bottom"}

## The equipment

![We apply an RF pulse to the substrate using an RF coil. The pulse is an oscillating signal at a particular frequency.  We then measure a voltage that comes from the substrate, using the same coil. Under the right conditions there is a signal emitted from the substrate following the RF excitation.](images/ch05/the-free-induction-decay-experiment-2.png){#fig-ch05-the-free-induction-decay-experiment-2 fig-cap-location="bottom"}

## The signal

![The voltage signal we measure is also an oscillating voltage, at the same frequency as the RF signal we applied. The response starts with a relatively high amplitude and decays over time.](images/ch05/the-free-induction-decay-experiment-3.png){#fig-ch05-the-free-induction-decay-experiment-3 fig-cap-location="bottom"}

:::
The experimental equipement and the signal from a free induction decay experiment.

Remember - at this point in our understanding we are not measuring an image!  We are measuring a time varying voltage signal from a beaker of water.  It will be a little while from now before we get to the topic of how we might form an image. The following material is all about measurements from a single volume.
